text: This is the lesson where Grover's algorithm stops being free lunch and becomes something you have to use correctly. Running extra iterations to be safe isn't harmless the way it would be for most algorithms — past a specific point, every additional iteration makes your answer more likely to be wrong, not less.

Each Grover iteration rotates the state by a fixed angle, 2 alpha, where sine of alpha equals 1 over root N. Since that rotation per step is fixed, there's one specific number of steps that gets you closest to the marked state: t star equals floor of pi over 4 alpha, approximately floor of pi over 4 times root N. Rotate too little and you haven't arrived yet; rotate too much and you've swung past it. And t star scaling as root N is exactly the source of the quadratic speedup — a million-fold larger search space needs only around 785 iterations, not a million.

Here's the full verified trajectory for N equals 8, one marked item. Starting probability is just the baseline guess, 12.5%. Iteration 1 climbs to 78.12%. Iteration 2 peaks at 94.53% — exactly matching the formula's prediction of t star equals 2. But iteration 3 falls to 33.01%, overshooting the target, and iteration 4 collapses all the way to 1.22% — worse than doing zero iterations at all. Two extra safety iterations don't just waste work, they actively destroy the result.

This happens because, unlike gradient descent or iterative refinement, there's no fixed point here — the rotation angle is constant every iteration, not shrinking, so the state keeps rotating past the marked state, around, and back toward where it started. The probability trajectory is periodic, not steadily improving. That means you must compute t star in advance and stop exactly there — there's no safety margin available by running a few more iterations, and for a million-item search, t star is exactly 785, with the same overshoot risk if you go past it.
Next lesson traces the whole algorithm by hand, on two worked examples, confirming the exact numbers you just saw and applying the same reasoning to a brand-new size.
